title: Perfect Number
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every integer up to num versus a square-root-bounded search that discovers both divisors of a pair at once.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a positive integer num, return true if it is a perfect number, that is, if the sum of all its positive divisors, excluding num itself, equals num, and false otherwise.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","num, a positive integer"],["Output","true if num equals the sum of its proper divisors, false otherwise"],["Goal","Decide this without listing every integer from 1 up to num minus 1"],["Constraints","1 <= num <= 100000000"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Every divisor of num pairs with a partner divisor","Search only up to the square root of num, discovering both divisors in a pair at once"],["The check is a single sum comparison","A simple accumulator, no need to store the divisors themselves"]]}

blocks.text: Given num, add up every positive integer that divides it evenly, other than num itself, and check whether that sum equals num.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Number That Exactly Equals the Sum of Its Own Parts
blocks.text: Picture splitting a number into every smaller piece that evenly divides it, then checking whether those pieces, added back together, exactly rebuild the original number, no more, no less.

blocks.caption: Divisors come in pairs: i and num / i are found together

blocks.text: The proper divisors of 28 are 1, 2, 4, 7, and 14, and 1 + 2 + 4 + 7 + 14 = 28, so the answer is true.
7 is prime, so its only proper divisor is 1, and 1 does not equal 7, so the answer is false.
1 has no proper divisors other than itself to exclude, so the sum of proper divisors is 0, not equal to 1, and the answer is false.
Before summing every integer up to num minus 1, notice that divisors of num always come in pairs that multiply back to num.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If i divides num evenly, then num divided by i is also a divisor, and the two are found together the moment i is found.

Observation 2: Once i exceeds the square root of num, its pair partner num divided by i would be smaller than i, meaning that pair has already been discovered from the smaller side.

Observation 3: Searching i only from 2 up to the square root of num, and adding both i and its partner whenever they differ, finds every proper divisor without ever checking values past the square root.

Observation 4: Starting the running sum at 1 accounts for the divisor 1 up front, since every number greater than 1 is divisible by 1.
This leads directly to a square-root-bounded search that discovers both divisors of a pair in a single check.
Check every integer from 1 up to num minus 1, adding it to a running sum whenever it divides num evenly, then compare the sum to num.

items: For every i from 1 to num minus 1, if num mod i is 0, add i to the sum.
Compare the final sum to num.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: check every candidate divisor individually

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every integer up to num minus 1 is checked individually, with no shortcuts.
The running sum accumulates every divisor found, in the order they are discovered.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(num), checking every integer up to num minus 1.
Space: O(1).
Limitation: for large num (up to 100000000), checking every single integer is far too slow, even though most divisors are discoverable in pairs well before num is reached.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every integer is wasteful: any divisor i greater than the square root of num always has a smaller partner divisor, num divided by i, that would already have been found earlier.

What does searching only up to the square root capture: every divisor pair, since one member of each pair is always at most the square root of num.

What about the case where i equals num divided by i: that happens only when num is a perfect square, and that shared value must be added only once, not twice.

The core idea: search i from 2 up to the square root of num, adding both i and num divided by i whenever they differ, starting the sum at 1 to account for that divisor up front.

Loop i from 2 while i times i is at most num. Whenever num mod i is 0, add i to the running sum, and also add num divided by i, unless the two are equal. Start the sum at 1 to include that divisor without a separate check.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: search only up to the square root, both divisors of a pair found together

blocks.text: Every divisor of num greater than its square root has a partner smaller than the square root, so scanning only up to the square root and adding both members of each pair discovers every proper divisor. The only care needed is not double-counting the square root itself when num is a perfect square.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(square root of num), a genuine complexity class improvement.
Space: O(1).

blocks.text: Perfect Number is a direct application of the classic divisor-pair trick: any divisor search only ever needs to check up to the square root, since every divisor beyond that point has already been found through its smaller partner.

blocks.text: Mentioning the divisor-pair symmetry, and why the search bound is the square root rather than num itself, is usually the fastest way to demonstrate the key optimization.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every integer up to num", think: divisors come in pairs, search only up to the square root.

Any divisor-finding or primality-testing problem that searches only up to the square root of the number.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(num) time; the optimized square-root search runs in O(square root of num) time. Both use O(1) space.

items: Pattern: square-root-bounded divisor search, exploiting the pairing between i and num divided by i.
Core Idea: every divisor beyond the square root has a smaller partner already found, so the search never needs to go past it.
Time: O(num) for the brute force, O(square root of num) for the optimized search.
Most Important Observation: divisors always come in pairs that multiply to num, one member of every pair is at most the square root.
Interview Difficulty: straightforward once the square-root bound and the perfect-square edge case are both recognized.
One line memory trick: divisors come in pairs, so only search up to the square root.
